title: Three Reminders From the First Week of School That I Really Needed
author: Marcus Luther
summary: Marcus Luther, a high school English teacher beginning his fifteenth year, reflects on a strong three-day opening week and the reminders it gave him. His first point is about locus of control: a new weekly mind-mapping practice revealed that his pre-year worries centered on school policies, district directives and AI debates, but once students arrived his attention snapped back to the classroom, the one space he can actually shape. His second is the pleasure and promise of reading student writing when students are given authentic, meaningful writing opportunities, even as the system often pulls in the other direction. The third reminder, prompted by a laminated note from a former student saying he made them feel recognized, is that students deserve to feel seen in every classroom, and he tried to plan backward from that priority. Luther closes by crediting a network of teachers for many of his practices, then offers his weekly "left in the copier" roundup with short commentary on six pieces, including Edutopia's bell ringers and veteran teachers keeping their cool, Brett Vogelsinger on balanced technology, Dylan Kane's Against Notes, Adrian Neibauer on attentive listening, and Matt Seybold on AI companies guillotining books.
points: Luther's weekly mind maps exposed how much of his pre-year anxiety concerned things outside his control, and the arrival of students re-centered him on what he can influence.
He argues it would be a travesty to let concerns that may eventually trickle down distract from the good already happening inside the classroom.
His enthusiasm for student writing is conditional on authentic, meaningful writing opportunities, which he says the education system too often works against.
Planning backward from the priority that students feel seen, prompted by a former student's note, is what he credits for the success of Week 1.
He attributes much of his classroom's improvement to an online community of teachers sharing practice, and uses a curated roundup to pass that learning on.
quotes: The week before students arrived, my mind map made it very clear that my mind was on things far beyond the classroom: school policies and leadership decisions, district directives and curriculum choices, and even broader thoughts around ongoing debates of AI, etc.

Then they did indeed show up and at once everything clicked into place: a good classroom is everything and students bring so much of that goodness in the door with them, in a way that no one not in the classroom can really understand.
That, after all, is something I can control as a teacher: staying present to the good taking place in the classroom right now, and Week 1 reaffirmed that continuously for me.

That said, I think it’s important to contextualize this enthusiasm a tad: I love reading student writing when they are writing in a way that is authentic and meaningful—and too often it feels like the gravity of our education system is pulling students in the opposite direction.

There are many ways to go about recognition in the classroom but underneath all those activities and strategies, I think, is the commitment to that priority: students deserve to feel seen in every classroom they step into.

I get that the word “community” can sound cliché given how often it is tossed around, but I don’t know a better word for what has emerged for me over the last half-decade: a network of folks consistently “talking shop” and sharing ideas about our classrooms and broader education policy.

Perhaps the most helpful thing amidst the “broader discourse” around things like screen usage in education is actual examples from actual teachers, and Brett’s generosity in interrogating his own choices around screens in his classroom?
